newsitem.title: USA: NY Assembly wants schools, police to get surcharge.
newsitem.headline: NY Assembly wants schools, police to get surcharge.

text.p: The New York Assembly Speaker on Monday proposed that New York City's 12.5 percent personal income tax surcharge, which ends at year-end unless it is extended by the legislature, be spent on police and schools.

The surcharge, which is expected to raise $455 million in the city's 1996 fiscal year and $473 million in the following year, first was approved to help the city fight crime and most of the revenues have gone toward that effort.
But starting on January 1, 1997, all of the tax revenues are supposed to be funneled into the General Fund, according to the city's budget.
Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, told the Citizens Crime Commission in the city he was confident the surcharge will be extended during a special, mid-December legislative session.

Saying tax revenues from the surcharge are expected to rise almost 50 percent or about $700 million over the next four years, Silver, in prepared remarks, said the Giuliani Administration should not go ahead with plans to cut the police force through attrition.

"We can make $1 billion available for school construction: at least $700 million in revenues from the personal income tax surcharge growth plus the $275 million budgeted by the mayor and the city council for school rehabilitiation in the 1997 fiscal year. At the same time, we can maintain police levels at the historic high of the last four years."
Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, a Republican, who wants the state legislature to extend the surcharge at its special session, did not appear to be inclined to oppose the state Democrat leader's proposal.
"The fact is New York City is operating the largest police force it ever had in its history and all of the money could easily be used for that," he told reporters at City Hall.

The Speaker of the Democrat-led City Council, Peter Vallone, previously proposed that the tax surcharge be set aside for schools, many of which badly need repairs, but Giuliani wanted the funds instead to go to the General Fund.

The importance placed on the views held by the Assembly Leader, whose Democratic party enjoys a clear majority in the Assembly, was underscored by the Council Chairman of the Finance Committee, Herbert Berman. Referring to Silver, he said: "Clearly, he's a major player, and clearly he has the ability if he choooses to exercize it, if he compels changes."
